description: You signed a waiver at the trampoline park, camp or party venue and your child got hurt. Why that may not end your child's claim under Georgia law.
shortAnswer: Georgia's appellate courts have not squarely decided whether a parent's signature on a waiver before an injury bars the child's own claim. “You signed a waiver” is the beginning of the conversation, not the end of it.

sections.heading: What the waiver says
sections.shortAnswer: You give up any claim against the business if your child is hurt, even if the business was careless. Many make you promise to pay the business back if your child ever sues it.

sections.heading: Georgia law on waivers in general
sections.shortAnswer: To be enforced, the waiver's language must be explicit, prominent, clear, and unambiguous. A waiver generally cannot release a business from liability for gross negligence, or for willful or wanton misconduct.

sections.heading: Can a parent sign away a child’s claim before the child is hurt?
sections.shortAnswer: This is the real question, and it is not settled in Georgia. Courts in other states have split.

sections.heading: What your signature may cost you
sections.shortAnswer: The waiver may be weaker against your child. It may be stronger against you. Read the waiver for an indemnity clause and an arbitration clause.

sections.heading: When your teenager signs
sections.shortAnswer: In Smith v. Adventure Air Sports Kennesaw, LLC, 357 Ga. App. 1 (2020), a 17-year-old signed his father's name. The Court of Appeals held he could not use his age to get out of the agreement.

sections.heading: The waiver does not cover everyone
sections.shortAnswer: A waiver usually protects the business that wrote it. If your child was hurt because a piece of equipment was defective, the company that made it did not get a waiver from you.

sections.heading: What I tell parents to do
sections.shortAnswer: Read the waiver and keep a copy. If your child is hurt, ask for a copy of what you signed, take pictures, and do not assume the waiver ended your child's claim.

faq.q: Does a waiver I signed at a trampoline park bar my child's injury claim in Georgia?
faq.a: It is not settled in Georgia. Georgia's appellate courts have not squarely decided whether a parent's signature on a waiver before an injury bars the child's own claim. It does mean that “you signed a waiver” is the beginning of the conversation, not the end of it.

faq.q: Why should a Georgia court protect a child despite a parent's waiver?
faq.a: When a settlement of a child's claim is more than $25,000, a parent cannot make it binding on the child without a court's approval. O.C.G.A. § 29-3-3. A minor's contract is generally voidable. O.C.G.A. § 13-3-20.

faq.q: Can a waiver protect a business from gross negligence?
faq.a: A waiver generally cannot release a business from liability for gross negligence, or for willful or wanton misconduct. A business that ignored known dangers, or broke basic safety rules, may not be able to hide behind the form.

faq.q: Does the waiver affect my own claim as a parent?
faq.a: The waiver may be weaker against your child. It may be stronger against you. You signed the waiver for yourself as an adult. The business will argue it bars your claim even if your child's survives.
